title: The kabitts
hook: Bhai Gurdas also wrote short Braj verses of great beauty

segments.voice: Yesterday, kikar, and your line, a hedge for the orchard. What small boundary did you plant, and what did it protect? Day seven hundred twelve.

Some writers have two voices. The same person who writes a long novel also scribbles tiny poems in the margins, and sometimes it's the tiny ones people carry around. For days now we've been walking through Bhai Gurdas's vars: long ballads, stanza after stanza, telling the story of the Gurus and the sangat. But that wasn't all he wrote. He had a second voice, in a second language, and it was small. Today: the kabitts.
screen: `TWO VOICES, ONE WRITER.` → `THE LONG BALLADS: THE VARS.` → `A SECOND VOICE, SMALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the language. The vars are in Punjabi. The kabitts are in Braj, a language of poetry, written down in the Gurmukhi script Sikhs use for the Guru's word. Bhai Gurdas could move between them. Then the shape. A kabitt is a short, tightly measured stanza. Where a var tells a story across many verses, a kabitt has to say what it says inside one. That changes how it works. A kabitt can't wander. It packs. One way Bhai Gurdas packs is by stacking pictures. As this, so that. As a thing in nature behaves, so a Sikh of the Guru behaves. Comparison after comparison, pressed close together, until the last line lands with all their weight behind it. A kabitt is less like a road and more like a jewel: you turn it over in your hand and the light catches a different face each time. Why does that matter? Because some truths need a story, and some need a stone you can carry. One way to hear it: the vars suit a long evening in the sangat, when there's time for the whole tale. The kabitts suit a pocket. Short enough to learn. Dense enough to keep giving. And there's a quiet lesson in the fact that he wrote both. The same devotion can be told long and told short. A whole life of praise, and a single bright line you can read aloud before the kettle boils.
screen: `PUNJABI VARS, BRAJ KABITTS.` · `ONE TIGHT STANZA.` · `AS THIS, SO THAT.` · `A STORY, OR A STONE TO CARRY.` · then, large: `SMALL AND BRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one of his verses aloud. If you can, find a single kabitt of Bhai Gurdas in a translation you trust, or one stanza of his vars if that's what's at hand. Don't hunt for long. Pick one. Then use the sit to read it slowly, out loud if you can, or under your breath. Read it a second time. Notice one picture in it, and let that picture sit in your mind while the bell runs. If there's no verse nearby, sit with the last line you remember from these lessons. The bell holds the time.
The kabitts. Bhai Gurdas's short verses in Braj, written in Gurmukhi: one tight stanza each, packed with pictures.
Your line: small and bright. Today, carry one short line you love, and read it once more before you sleep. Day seven hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Bhai Gurdas's Kabitt Savaiye are studied and recited by Sikhs alongside his vars, and some are sung in kirtan.

notes: No count of kabitts is given (sources vary). Confirm that 'Braj, a language of poetry' is a fair gloss.
The 'jaise ... taise' (as this, so that) stacking of comparisons is described as one of his techniques; confirm.
'For days now we've been walking through Bhai Gurdas's vars' refers to this path's own days 697–711 (fifteen days); confirm the phrasing is acceptable.
No kabitt is quoted or paraphrased, since no public-domain English translation could be confirmed. A Keeper may wish to name one kabitt for the practice.
howItsDone: confirm 'some are sung in kirtan'.

Audit (2026-10-01): cut the filler line 'those who love them speak of their beauty'. The teach stays abstract because no kabitt could be paraphrased safely; a Keeper-chosen kabitt (one picture, paraphrased, with its number) would lift this day most.
